text: The condemned man is not the subject of this film; the warden who signs off on his execution is. Bernadine Williams has overseen enough of them that the procedure now lives in her body. Chinonye Chukwu builds the picture out of protocol — the checklists, the rehearsals, the institutional calm a state killing requires in order to pass for a job done correctly — and that calm is where the dread sits. Sundance's dramatic jury gave it their prize, and the reason is legible in the restraint: 112 minutes of pressure kept interior, registered in a face working hard to give nothing away. What stands to be lost is not only a life. It is Bernadine's capacity to keep signing off on this and still be a person who goes home in the evening and sits down to dinner.

Eighty-five minutes, three stories, and no agreement among them about what kind of film this is. One strand takes a killing inside a suburban family and reports the aftermath as a miracle. Another turns a scientist's experiment into contagion, and the picture into a monster movie. The third stays in a prison, on two men and the fixation that binds them. Todd Haynes cuts among the three instead of lining them up, so horror, crime report and love story keep interrupting one another before any of them can settle into a tone. Drama, horror and science fiction all sit on its record, and all three are honest. The transgression is less in any single image than in the refusal to keep those registers in separate rooms. Sundance's Grand Jury Prize and a Teddy Award followed.

A young man wants to make his first film, and the money turns out to be in the pocket of someone who should not be trusted with it. Alexandre Rockwell gets ninety-six minutes of comedy out of that arrangement, in which the gangster is less an obstacle than an enthusiast: a man delighted to be adjacent to art and entirely unclear about what it costs. Sundance gave the film its dramatic Grand Jury Prize and a separate award for acting, and the second is the more telling of the two. Nothing happens here that is not two people talking each other into something. What stands to be lost is not the money, which was never really the filmmaker's, but the film he would have made had he waited for a duller patron.

A quinceañera is planned a year out: the dress, the hall, a family's account of what a girl becomes at fifteen. This one arrives with the celebrant already carrying news that voids the terms. Richard Glatzer films the consequence rather than the scandal. Magdalena is put out of the house and taken in by a great-granduncle and a cousin whose own standing in the family is conditional, and the ninety minutes that follow are largely about the household those three assemble out of people the rite had no plans for. Fifteen is the age the ceremony marks, and it is also the age at which she is expected to manage all of it. Shot in Spanish in the United States, close enough to one neighborhood to make the closeness a method. Both the dramatic jury at Sundance and the audience there chose it.

Three women leave, or try to, and Rebecca Miller gives each of them under half an hour. The arithmetic is the design: eighty-six minutes split three ways forbids the long approach, so every story opens with the arrangement already failing and closes before the consequences have finished arriving. What the compression buys is comparison. Set side by side, the three exits rhyme without matching, since one woman's leverage is money, another's is work, another's is only distance, and those differences argue better than a single portrait could. Miller does not pretend the escapes are equivalent, or that any of them is finished when the vignette stops. Stated flat, the premise sounds thin: women getting out from under men. The structure is what turns it into a proposition rather than a slogan.

A chemistry set in a bedroom in suburban London in the 1960s, in the hands of a boy no one has thought to watch closely. Benjamin Ross plays what follows as comedy, and that choice is the entire film: Graham Young's loathing of his stepmother and his gift for compounds get the same deadpan attention, one appetite among others in a house where nothing interesting is supposed to occur. The tone holds because the boy is otherwise unremarkable, dull even, in every respect but the one. Much of the ninety-nine minutes goes to the small pleasures of method: measurement, patience, a plan that requires no strength at all to carry out. The comedy is not a softening. It is the instrument that lets the film stay this close to him without flinching and without explaining.

For most of its length this is a film about a fifteen-year-old with nothing to do. The mall, the beach, a driveway, a family that has already settled which daughter she is — Joyce Chopra spends real time on the boredom, on the way Connie practices a voice and a walk that are not yet hers and tries them out where it looks safe. Listing the film as both drama and thriller is accurate, and it also describes the shape: attention gathers in flirtations that are not events, until one of them is. What makes the first hour matter is that Chopra never treats it as filler. It came out of Sundance with the dramatic jury's prize. Boredom, here, is the condition that makes a stranger's interest feel like being seen at last.

Lotus harvesting, pedaling a cyclo, hawking trinkets to tourists: the film organizes a city around the work done in it. Ho Chi Minh City at the end of the nineties is changing faster than any of those trades can follow, and Tony Bui lets that pressure arrive through hours and wages instead of speeches about modernity. The strands touch lightly. An American who left a daughter behind when the war ended has come back to look for her; a driver has fallen for a woman whose time costs more than he earns; a boy loses the case that holds his living. It plays in Vietnamese, as Ba Mùa, and went forward as an international submission to the Academy Awards. At Sundance both the audience and the dramatic jury picked it.

Ruby Lee Gissing takes a job in a souvenir shop, and Victor Nuñez treats the hiring as the event it is. A hundred and fourteen minutes is a long stretch to grant a young woman whose only plan was leaving, and that is exactly the resource the film spends: on shifts and rent, on the arithmetic of a Florida tourist town, on the distance between a man who is charming and a man who is kind. The romance is present and is not the engine. What she is testing is whether a life can be assembled out of a wage, a room, and a few people who are decent to her, after a death shoved her out of the last one. Sundance's dramatic jury gave it the Grand Jury Prize.

Two coworkers, one apartment, one evening: that is the whole allotment of incident. Tom Noonan takes ninety-one minutes for a dinner arranged between two people from the same law office, an evening with the shape of a date and none of its assurances, and the film has nowhere to go but into what gets said, misheard, revised and said again. The Waldo Salt Screenwriting Award it took at Sundance is the honest one to cite: every line is load-bearing, and the comedy and the dread come off the same sentences depending on which of the two is listening. A chamber piece this size stands or falls on two performances, and the exposure shows in every scene. What one dinner can cost is small and not small at all: an evening, and whichever version of themselves the two brought to it.

Memphis, a house paid for by music recorded decades ago, and inside it a woman who arrived from Russia into a life already fully furnished. Ira Sachs keeps her at the edges of rooms where her husband is the reason everyone else has come, and the method is to watch what a person does with the hours in which nothing is required of her. The son's visit supplies the disturbance. By the standards of drama it is a small one, a grown child with old grievances staying a while, and Sachs declines to inflate it. The film measures a marriage in errands and silences instead. The awakening the premise promises is not a scene but an accumulation, and the hundred and eight minutes are the argument that it could not have been reached any faster.

William Douglas Street solves the problem of his life by becoming other people, and each impersonation is handled as a species of employment. Bored working for his father, pressed for money at home, he goes out as a reporter, then a doctor, then a lawyer, and the thing Wendell B. Harris Jr. keeps noticing is how little resistance the world puts up against a man who speaks with authority. The disguises are not costumes; they are vocabularies, acquired the way other men acquire tools. Ninety-four minutes, made in 1989, and the comedy takes its edge from tracking precisely which credentials go unchecked, and for whom. The Sundance jury gave it the dramatic Grand Jury Prize. It is a crime picture whose crime is fluency, and it is funniest exactly where that ought to be alarming.

Every summer the two sisters are handed over to the same house in Las Cruces, and every summer their father has to be learned again. Alessandra Lacorazza builds the film out of those visits and the gaps between them, so the daughters arrive older each time and he is met in whatever state the year has left him in. The ellipses carry the weight. Nothing accounts for the ten months off screen; the evidence sits in the furniture, in what the girls will and will not ask him, in how long a pause runs before anyone answers. He is loving and he is unreliable, and In the Summers refuses to settle that into a verdict, which is the harder position to hold across ninety-eight minutes. It came out of Sundance with the U.S. Dramatic Grand Jury Prize.

Two strangers turn up in Brooklyn with the same claim on the same man, and only one of them is his son. Christopher Zalla builds the thriller on the single thing his young protagonist cannot produce: proof. No papers, no history anyone will check, only a boy's word against a practiced man's in a city with no reason to care which of them is true. The crossing itself is over early; what the film wants is the arrival and the days after it. Its cruelty is administrative rather than violent, a matter of who gets believed and how fast a father settles the question. What the impostor wants is money. What the boy came for can be neither stolen from him nor demonstrated. It carries a Sundance Grand Jury Prize and an Academy Awards international submission on its record.
